purpose: Latency and energy per connection type, graded by what is actually known. The connection library had `delay_class` with three symbolic values and `parameters` with no unit attached, so an optimiser could only trade one axis -- structure -- and the Phase 3 computation result measured negative for a reason that was in the vocabulary all along. This artifact adds the numbers where a citation exists and `unknown` where one does not.

grades.bounded: a defensible range from cited literature
grades.derived: computed from another measured field in this library

cost_axis.name: axo_dendritic
cost_axis.latency_note: Guyton & Hall 2008 (p.570) gives 0.5 ms as the minimum synaptic delay; standard physiology quotes 0.5-4 ms typical, and the upper end reaches 5 ms for a large-conductance release. The range is kept rather than a midpoint because the variance IS the trade: a generator choosing a fast synapse is trading against reliability.

energy.note: vesicle cycling + receptor work + ion gradients

cost_axis.name: modulatory_diffuse
cost_axis.latency_note: Volume transmission is slow by construction: the signal is a diffusion cloud, so onset scales with distance and the peak is orders of magnitude later than a synaptic event. The 10-1000 ms band is a spread, not a measurement of one receptor -- the point is that the spread IS the mechanism, and a generator that wants a slow global state has no cheaper way to get one.

energy.note: one release reaches many targets; per-target cost is low but the release itself is not free

cost_axis.citation: Herkenham & Substance 1990 on volume transmission; Bargmann 2012, Current Opinion in Neurobiology

cost_axis.name: neuromodulatory_axon
cost_axis.latency_note: A spike travelling an axon is a conduction problem, not a connection problem. Conduction velocity is range- and temperature-dependent in insects, so no single value is defensible here and none is invented. What a generator can still use is the structural cost below, which is counted in the library.

energy.note: maintaining a long axon is metabolically costly; this is the term the -84% wire-cost result exploited

cost_axis.citation: T-buron et al.; standard invertebrate conduction textbooks -- deliberately not quoted as a number because the range is too wide to be useful

cost_axis.name: gap_junction_sync

The comparison that matters for the generator: an electrical synapse is 2.5-80x faster than a chemical one, and it is bidirectional, which is a topological property no delay number captures.

energy.note: no vesicle cycle, no receptor trafficking

cost_axis.citation: Guyton & Hall 2008, Ch. 46 (electrical synapses); Bloom & O'Boyle 2013 review of connexin transmission

caveat: Latency here is the delay attributable to the connection, not a path latency. Compose per-type delays to get a path; a circuit motif therefore has no latency of its own and says so.

Energy is a relative trichotomy (cheap / typical / expensive), not joules. A per-spike joule figure needs cell-type and temperature corrections this library does not have, and a wrong absolute number is worse than an honest relative one.

21 of the 66 types are `abstraction_only` design patterns. They get no physiological number by construction; their `delay_class` is kept under `designed_cost` so an assumption is never summed with a measurement.

The fastest electrical synapse is asserted to be strictly faster than the slowest chemical one and the script refuses to write if that stops holding -- the whole trade the axis exists to express depends on it.

These values characterise biology. They do not say what a generated topology should cost: choosing a fast, faithful, cheap electrical link everywhere would be a design decision, and the library's own Phase 3 evidence is that a compute advantage does not follow from the biological prior.
